source.title: More is Better in Modern Machine Learning: when Infinite Overparameterization is Optimal and Overfitting is Obligatory
source.authors: James B. Simon; Dhruva Karkada; Nikhil Ghosh; Mikhail Belkin

record.file_problem: Text is the full paper with appendices; some figure text is garbled, but the surrounding descriptions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests interpolation and fitting behavior in kernel ridge regression and random-feature regression, and explicitly limits conclusions about deep networks to kernel-regime models rather than SGD-trained networks.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own random-feature and KRR experiments on CIFAR10 and four vision datasets. The paper does not test completely random labels, shuffled or Gaussian inputs, optimizer-time costs, explicit regularizers, or learning order. Cited findings are not rows. Values recoverable only from plots are not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The study examines optimal regularization and generalization in random-feature regression and KRR. It does not test any claim version: optimality of interpolation under Gaussian regression-label noise differs from whether standard deep networks can fit randomly corrupted class labels. A nonzero optimal training error does not demonstrate an inability to interpolate.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. Within their risk-estimate framework, the authors establish benefits of more samples and features at optimal ridge, and obligatory overfitting for suitable powerlaw KRR tasks. Vision experiments support near-interpolation optimality and negligible intrinsic noise, while added Gaussian label noise increases the optimal fitting ratio. These conclusions concern RF/KRR models and optimal generalization, not random-class-label fitting by ordinary SGD-trained deep networks.
record.recipe_differences: Uses closed-form risk estimates and kernel ridge regression with convolutional neural tangent kernels, plus random-feature regression experiments; no SGD-trained deep network or random-label intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Added label noise changes the optimal fitting ratio from approximately zero to nonzero; the paper states it increases with added noise. The curves are shown at multiple relative noise levels.

fits_no_version.finding: On clean vision tasks, convolutional-NTK KRR achieves optimal test MSE near interpolation; adding Gaussian label-vector noise raises the test-optimal fitting ratio.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For convolutional-NTK KRR, the optimal amount of fitting depends on task eigenstructure and regression-label noise.

fits_no_version.finding: At optimally tuned ridge, increasing random-feature count improves test performance, with measured train and test errors closely matching the risk estimates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More random features improve generalization in the tested ridge-regression settings when regularization is tuned optimally.

record.problems: The central results are for KRR and random-feature regression rather than SGD-trained deep networks. The RF risk derivation is described as nonrigorous and uses a Gaussian universality ansatz; several experimental values appear only in figures, and Appendix D reports a post-hoc vertical fit for theory curves.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying result rows were omitted. Figure 1 and Figure 3 compare random-feature regression against its risk framework; the summarized outcomes are included in R9. Other cited results are prior work, not this study's results.

untested.parts: SGD-trained standard deep networks fitting completely random class labels with unchanged architecture and hyperparameters, including chance test error.
Training-time comparison between real and random labels and convergence-speed changes across corruption fractions.
Deep-network fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs. Synthetic Gaussian regression inputs here carry a structured linear target.
Perfect training fit and steadily increasing test error toward chance across a sweep from zero to complete random class-label corruption in deep networks.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting, and true-label generalization after removing those regularizers.
Training trajectories showing shared real-data patterns learned before noisy or random labels.

record.verdict_notes: Remove both V4 verdicts. Clean-label interpolation optimality does not support V4's noise-sweep claim, and choosing nonzero training error for optimal generalization does not limit V4's claim that noisy training labels can be fit.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment trains a standard deep network with SGD on completely random labels, or measures chance test error under that condition.
No comparison of training time for true versus random labels, nor a sweep over the fraction of corrupted labels measuring convergence speed.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment.

Tests KRR on vision tasks with added Gaussian label noise and reports that optimal fitting ratio becomes nonzero as noise is added; does not test random label corruption through 100%, steady test-error increase across corruption fractions, or simultaneous perfect training fit throughout.
No test of weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation on fitting random labels or generalizing on true labels.
No training-trajectory comparison of learning real-label structure before noisy or random labels.

rows.subject: Random-feature regression with Gaussian data and random ReLU features on CIFAR10
rows.stage_stated: only the second layer trained (random-feature regression)
rows.operation_detail: Random-feature regression across varying number of features and ridge; CIFAR10 binary classification with random ReLU features.
rows.measure: Train and test MSE as number of random features varies at optimal ridge.
rows.value: At optimal ridge, more features monotonically improves test performance; measured errors closely match the theoretical predictions.
rows.note: This result concerns feature-count scaling and RF risk, not label corruption; included as an own reported outcome bearing only indirectly on fitting behavior, and does not establish V4.
rows.check: Feature-count scaling at optimal ridge tests none of the versions. The subject also conflates two separate experiments: synthetic Gaussian inputs with linear Gaussian projection features, and CIFAR10 images with random ReLU features. Split these if retained as contextual results.
